WPILib: built in, no app

The whole follower fits on one slide

deck10/WpilibPaths.java

  public static Command follow(

      CANDriveSubsystem drive, Trajectory path) {

1   var follower = new LTVUnicycleController(0.02);

    follower.setEnabled(USE_FEEDBACK);

    Timer clock = new Timer();

    return drive.startRun(() -> {

2         drive.resetPose(path.getInitialPose());

          clock.restart();

        }, () -> {

3         Trajectory.State plan = path.sample(clock.get());

          drive.driveSpeeds(

4             follower.calculate(drive.getPose(), plan));

        })

        .withTimeout(path.getTotalTimeSeconds())

        .finallyDo(drive::stop);

  }

1

The follower

LTVUnicycleController is WPILib’s follower for tank drives.

2

Start at the start

Tell odometry the robot is at the first point.

3

Sample the plan

The target pose and speed for this moment.

4

Feedforward plus feedback

The planned speed, plus a fix for the pose error.

6

What you need first

Every library needs these, and a stock KitBot has none

You needWhat it doesStock 2026 KitBot
Wheel encodersMeasure how far each side rolledNone. CIMs have no built-in encoder
GyroMeasures which way the robot pointsNone in the build or the code
OdometryTurns those into a pose on the fieldNothing to feed it
Tuned drivetrainDrives at the speed you ask forNot yet: stick to volts, nothing measured

You can add them. The KitBot gearboxes have holes for optional encoders. Measure kV and kS with WPILib’s SysId tool.

Best practice

Start with a timed auto

Get a timed auto working first. It needs no sensors and no library.

FIRST’s KitBot code works this way. This one moved 2.5 m in our simulator, but carpet and battery change that, so measure on a real floor.

public static Command driveForward(CANDriveSubsystem drive) {

  return drive.driveArcade(() -> 0.6, () -> 0.0).withTimeout(1.5)

      .andThen(drive.runOnce(drive::stop))

      .andThen(Commands.print("launch fuel here"));

}

8

PathPlanner and Choreo

One lets you draw the path, one solves it

PathPlanner: you shape the curve

Drag Bézier curves in an app. That is a smooth line you bend with handles.

The timing is worked out on the robot, from your speed limits.

It can plan around obstacles during a match.

The follower comes with the library.

Choreo: a solver finds the fastest path

Place waypoints and limits in an app, and a solver does the rest.

The fastest path your drivetrain can do, saved to a fixed file.

Better robot numbers give better paths: mass, motors, gearing.

You write the follower yourself.

2       pathFollower(),

        robotConfig(),

3       PathPlannerPaths::isRedAlliance,

4   NamedCommands.registerCommand("launch", launch());

Choreo 2026.0.3

Choreo: you write the follower, then wire the routine

deck10/ChoreoPaths.java

// You write the follower. Choreo hands you one sample per loop.

private void follow(DifferentialSample sample) {

  ChassisSpeeds plan = sample.getChassisSpeeds();

  drive.driveSpeeds(follower.calculate(drive.getPose(), sample.getPose(),

      plan.vxMetersPerSecond, plan.omegaRadiansPerSecond));

}

 

public AutoRoutine toHubAndLaunch() {

  AutoRoutine routine = factory.newRoutine("toHubAndLaunch");

  AutoTrajectory toHub = routine.trajectory("toHub"); // deploy/choreo/toHub.traj

  routine.active().onTrue(Commands.sequence(toHub.resetOdometry(), toHub.cmd()));

  toHub.atTime("spinUp").onTrue(Commands.print("spin up")); // a marker from the app

  toHub.done().onTrue(Commands.print("launch fuel here"));

  return routine;

}

BLine 0.9.3: newest of the four

BLine: PID loops chase targets, with no timed plan

deck10/BLinePaths.java

  public static Command toHub(SwerveStandIn drive) {

    var follow = new FollowPath.Builder(

4       drive, drive::getPose,

        drive::getRobotRelativeSpeeds,

        drive::driveRobotRelative,

1       new PIDController(5.0, 0.0, 0.0), // translation

1       new PIDController(3.0, 0.0, 0.0), // rotation

1       new PIDController(2.0, 0.0, 0.0)) // cross-track

        .withPoseReset(drive::resetPose);

    FollowPath.registerEventTrigger("spinUp", spinUp());

    return follow.build(new Path(

2       new Path.Waypoint(2.0, 4.0, Rotation2d.kZero),

2       new Path.TranslationTarget(3.5, 4.5),

3       new Path.EventTrigger(0.5, "spinUp"),

2       new Path.Waypoint(5.0, 5.0, Rotation2d.kZero)));

  }

1

Three PID loops

Speed along the path, heading, and staying on the line.

2

Straight legs

The robot heads for each target, then hands off to the next.

3

Events

They fire part way along a leg.

4

Holonomic only

That means no tank. This code uses a swerve stand-in.

14

Common mistake

The path is correct, but the start pose is wrong

What you see

The curve looks right and the logs say the robot hit its target, but the real robot misses.

Why it happens

Resetting odometry sets the pose to the value you give. The robot can’t detect a wrong placement.

The fix

Measure your starting pose, and line up the same way every match. In sim, 10° crooked ended 55 cm off.

15

Exercise

Follow a path, then add a fault

1.

Run WPILib: Simulate Robot Code. In AdvantageScope, drag SimPose and TargetPose onto Poses.

2.

Click Autonomous in Robot State. When the robot stops, read Path ended in the VS Code terminal.

3.

In Constants, set LEFT_SIDE_STRENGTH to 0.9. Run it again and read the number.

4.

Now also set USE_FEEDBACK to false. Run it again and read the number.

Done when: you have three end errors, one from each run.

16

Recap

What this deck covered

A follower is Deck 6 with a moving setpoint: feedforward from a plan, feedback on pose error.

No encoders and gyro means no path following, so start with a timed auto.

PathPlanner draws paths, Choreo solves them, BLine chases targets, and WPILib gives you the parts.

For most young teams: timed auto, then PathPlanner, then Choreo when speed is your limit.
